Christians confess we do not live it perfectly, which is why morality in Scripture always walks hand in hand with mercy: the law shows us our need, and grace meets it.
RelatedEvents: The Ten Commandments; Sermon on the Mount

Summary: Myths are traditional stories that explain the world, and the Bible's relationship to them is more interesting than simple rejection. Some biblical stories share shapes with ancient myths - floods, heroes, creation battles - but retell them with a decisive difference: one Creator, a good creation, and a God who acts in real history. Christians also ask whether myths can carry truth: C. S. Lewis called the gospel a myth become fact, a story with myth's power that actually happened.

Nations in Scripture are more than political units: God made the peoples, scattered them, judges them, and promises to gather them. The Old Testament moves between God's particular love for Israel and His universal purpose for all nations, and Revelation ends with people from every tribe and tongue worshiping together. For Christians, this relativizes every national loyalty: our deepest citizenship is in heaven, and no nation is the kingdom of God.

Nature is God's first book, displaying His power and care to everyone, everywhere. Scripture treats creation as good, ordered, and purposeful - not divine itself, and not an accident - and calls humans its stewards, not its owners. Nature also witnesses against us: its beauty points to a Creator, and its brokenness groans under the same curse that afflicts us, waiting for the renewal promised in Christ.

A neighbor, Jesus taught, is not a category of person but anyone in need whom we have the power to help - including the stranger and the enemy. The parable of the Good Samaritan redefines neighborliness from proximity to mercy: seeing, stopping, and spending yourself for someone else's good. Loving neighbor is how love for God becomes visible, and Scripture insists it includes the poor, the foreigner, the widow, and the outsider.
RelatedQuestions: How can I love difficult people?

Summary: New life is the fresh start God gives through faith in Christ: the old self buried, a new self raised. The New Testament describes it with several pictures - new birth, new creation, resurrection - all pointing to the same reality: forgiveness of sins and the Spirit's power to live differently. New life begins in a moment but grows over a lifetime, as believers learn to walk in step with the Spirit and put off the old patterns of sin.

The Nicene Creed is the church's ancient summary of the faith, forged at Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381 to defend the full deity of Christ against Arianism. In a few hundred words it confesses one God, Jesus Christ as true God and true man, and the Holy Spirit as Lord and giver of life. Christians across traditions still recite it as a boundary of orthodoxy and a shared confession that predates every modern denomination.

Obedience is doing what God asks because we trust the One who asks it. Scripture never treats it as a cold duty: in Deuteronomy it flows from remembering deliverance, in the Psalms from delight in God's law, and in John's Gospel from love for Jesus. Obedience is also where faith becomes visible - Abraham leaving home, Mary saying let it be, Jesus in Gethsemane - and where blessing, discipline, and formation all meet.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 6:4-9; 1 Samuel 15:22; Psalm 119:1-8; Luke 1:38; John 14:15; Hebrews 5:8-9
RelatedBooks: Deuteronomy; 1 Samuel; Psalms; Luke; John; Hebrews

Summary: The occult covers practices that seek hidden knowledge or power apart from God: divination, spiritism, magic, and astrology. Scripture forbids them consistently, not because they are harmless superstition but because they open doors to spiritual realities God has not given us to traffic in. The Christian answer is not fascination or fear but trust: God's Word and Spirit give all the guidance we need, and Christ's authority is greater than any power the occult claims.

The Old Testament is the first three-quarters of the Christian Bible: law, history, poetry, and prophecy spanning from creation to the return from exile. Christians read it as God's own story, not as background material - the promises, patterns, and problems that the New Testament claims Jesus fulfills. Reading it well means honoring its genres, its ancient context, and its central arc: a holy God pursuing a wandering people.
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile

Summary: Origins asks where everything came from: the universe, life, and humanity itself. The Bible answers with a Creator who made all things good and purposeful, while Christians differ on how Genesis relates to scientific accounts of deep time and evolution. What unites orthodox Christians is the core confession: the universe is not an accident, human beings bear God's image, and creation's order reflects a rational Creator - convictions that made modern science itself possible.
RelatedQuestions: Did God create the world in six literal days?

Summary: Persecution is hostility faced for following Christ, from mockery and exclusion to imprisonment and death. Jesus promised it plainly and called it blessed, and the New Testament treats it as normal for a church that lives differently from the world around it. Christians respond not with retaliation but with endurance, prayer for enemies, and solidarity with suffering brothers and sisters - and by counting the cost honestly before promising the world that faith is easy.

Perseverance is the steady continuance of faith through trials, doubts, and long obedience - and, in Reformed theology, the conviction that God preserves His people to the end. Scripture holds both sides: believers must endure, and God is the one who keeps them enduring. The warnings against falling away and the promises that nothing can separate us from God's love are not contradictions but partners, urging vigilance without despair.
KeyPassages: John 10:27-29; Romans 8:28-39; Philippians 1:6; Hebrews 10:35-39; James 1:2-4; Revelation 2:10
RelatedQuestions: Can a Christian be sanctified and still struggle with sin?
RelatedBooks: John; Romans; Philippians; Hebrews; James; Revelation

Summary: Philosophy is the love of wisdom: asking the big questions about truth, goodness, beauty, and existence with reasoned argument. Scripture engages philosophy rather than ignoring it - Paul debated Stoics and Epicureans in Athens, and the church has used philosophical tools to clarify doctrines like the Trinity ever since. The Christian posture is discerning: all truth is God's truth, but human wisdom must bow to revelation where the two conflict, and reason serves faith rather than ruling it.

Pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place, undertaken to seek God, remember His acts, or mark a turning point. Israel's feasts drew pilgrims to Jerusalem three times a year, and Christians have walked to sites of biblical memory ever since - while remembering that the destination is a person, not a place. The Christian life itself is often described as pilgrimage: strangers and exiles traveling toward a heavenly country, learning dependence one step at a time.

Preaching is the public proclamation of God's Word, calling hearers to believe and obey. From the prophets to the apostles to the church today, preaching has carried a double weight: faithfully explaining the text and urgently applying it to real lives. Good preaching is not performance but stewardship - the preacher stands under the Word before standing before the people, and the goal is never admiration but transformation.

The presence of God is His nearness to His people - in the tabernacle's cloud, in the temple, in Jesus' incarnation, and now in the Spirit dwelling within believers. Scripture holds together God's everywhere-presence with His special, covenant presence: He is never absent, yet He draws near in worship, in suffering, and in obedience. The Christian hope is presence made permanent: one day we will see Him face to face, and the ache of distance will end.
KeyPassages: Exodus 33:14-16; Psalm 16:11; Psalm 139:7-12; Matthew 28:20; John 14:16-17; Revelation 21:1-4
RelatedEvents: The Burning Bush; Giving of the Law at Sinai; Pentecost

Summary: Pride is the inflated sense of self that puts us at the center where God belongs - the root sin behind the fall and the quiet engine of most others. Scripture warns that God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble, and it prescribes the cures: remembering we are creatures, receiving everything as gift, and serving others. Humility is not thinking less of ourselves but thinking of ourselves less, because our eyes are fixed on Christ.
KeyPassages: Proverbs 16:18; Isaiah 14:12-15; Daniel 4:28-37; Luke 18:9-14; James 4:6; 1 Peter 5:5-6
RelatedBooks: Proverbs; Isaiah; Daniel; Luke; James; 1 Peter

Summary: A promise is a word you can build a life on, and the Bible is held together by God's promises: to Abraham, to David, to Israel, and finally to all who trust in Christ. Unlike human promises, God's cannot fail, because they rest on His character rather than on circumstances. The Christian life is learning to live between promise and fulfillment - trusting what God has said while waiting for what He has not yet done.

The promises of God are His sworn commitments scattered through Scripture - hundreds of them, covering provision, presence, forgiveness, guidance, and eternal life. Christians read them as a family inheritance: every promise finds its yes in Christ, and each one invites trust in a specific situation. The discipline is to claim promises as God gave them, without twisting them into guarantees He never made or ignoring the conditions He attached.
KeyPassages: Genesis 28:15; Deuteronomy 31:6; Isaiah 41:10; Matthew 28:20; Romans 8:28; Hebrews 13:5-6
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Deuteronomy; Isaiah; Matthew; Romans; Hebrews

Summary: Provision is God's care for the material needs of His creatures, from manna in the wilderness to daily bread in the Lord's Prayer. Scripture ties it to both trust and work: God provides, and His people labor, share, and steward what they receive. Provision is never promised as luxury, and it is never merely spiritual - the God who feeds ravens and clothes lilies notices what His children need and meets it, often through other people's hands.
RelatedEvents: Wilderness Wanderings; Feeding of the Five Thousand

Summary: Psychology is the scientific study of mind and behavior, and Christians ask how its findings relate to Scripture's wisdom about human nature. Much of psychology describes God's design accurately - how habits form, how trauma wounds, how relationships heal - while its theories about ultimate meaning sometimes conflict with biblical anthropology. The Christian approach is integration without surrender: receive genuine insight gratefully, test every claim against Scripture, and remember that people are souls as well as systems.

Reason is the God-given capacity to think clearly, weigh evidence, and follow arguments where they lead. Christianity has always claimed that faith is not against reason: Paul reasoned in the synagogues, and the church's greatest thinkers argued that truth cannot contradict truth. Reason has limits - it cannot by itself grasp grace or resurrect the dead - but it is a servant of faith, clearing away bad arguments and helping believers love God with all their minds.

Reasoning is the practice of thinking well: forming beliefs for good reasons, spotting fallacies, and changing your mind when the evidence requires it. Scripture commends it - the Bereans examined the Scriptures daily to test what they heard - and warns against its counterfeits, like rationalization and cleverness in service of pride. For Christians, good reasoning is a spiritual discipline: it protects the church from error, sharpens witness, and honors a God who is Himself the Logos, the divine Reason.

Reconciliation is the restoration of a broken relationship, and in Scripture it is first God's work toward us: while we were enemies, Christ died to bring us back. That vertical reconciliation creates a horizontal one - Jew and Gentile, offender and offended, enemies made one new people - and the church is entrusted with its ministry. Reconciliation is not pretending nothing happened; it is truth, repentance, forgiveness, and rebuilt trust, in that costly order.
RelatedEvents: Joseph and His Brothers; The Prodigal Son

Summary: Reform is the church's recurring work of returning to Scripture when tradition, power, or complacency have pulled it off course. From Josiah's rediscovered law to the Protestant Reformers' recovery of grace, reform movements share a pattern: a fresh encounter with God's Word, repentance for accumulated error, and costly resistance from those who benefit from the status quo. Reform reminds every generation that the church is always in need of renewal - and that renewal begins with repentance, not with rebranding.

The Reformation was the sixteenth-century movement that reshaped Western Christianity, sparked by Martin Luther's protest against indulgences and carried forward by reformers across Europe. Its rallying cries - Scripture alone, grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, God's glory alone - recovered the gospel of free grace for millions and split the Western church. Its legacy is contested: renewal and division in the same event, and modern Christians inherit both the recovered truths and the responsibility to pursue unity without surrendering them.

Reformed theology is the tradition flowing from John Calvin and the Reformation, organized around God's sovereignty in salvation: grace that initiates, sustains, and completes redemption. Its landmarks include the five points of Calvinism, covenant theology, and confessions like Westminster, all emphasizing that salvation is God's work from first to last. Reformed Christians differ from other believers mainly on the mechanics of grace - election, atonement's extent, and perseverance - while sharing the same gospel of Christ crucified.
RelatedDoctrines: Election; Predestination; Perseverance of the Saints

Summary: Regeneration is the Spirit's work of giving new spiritual life to a dead heart - the new birth Jesus described to Nicodemus. It is monergistic in Reformed language: God acts first, and our faith and repentance follow as the fruit, not the cause. Regeneration is instantaneous and invisible, but its effects are visible over time: new desires, new loves, and a new direction that theologians call sanctification.

Relativism is the claim that truth, especially moral truth, depends on the individual or culture - true for you, but not for me. It feels tolerant, but it collapses under its own weight: the claim that there is no absolute truth is itself stated absolutely, and it leaves no ground to condemn real evils. Christians answer with both conviction and grace: truth is one and knowable, because it is grounded in God's character, and that conviction frees us to listen patiently rather than forcing agreement.

Repentance is the turning of the whole person - mind, heart, and direction - away from sin and toward God. It begins with honest recognition, includes sorrow for sin itself rather than merely its consequences, and proves itself in changed behavior: Zacchaeus repaid what he stole, and John the Baptist demanded fruit worthy of repentance. Repentance is not a one-time event but the rhythm of the Christian life, and it is always met by a Father who runs to meet returning children.
KeyPassages: Psalm 51:1-17; Isaiah 55:6-7; Luke 15:11-32; Luke 19:1-10; Acts 2:37-39; 2 Corinthians 7:10
RelatedEvents: Jonah and Nineveh; The Prodigal Son; David and Bathsheba

Summary: Respectful dialogue is conversation that honors the other person as made in God's image, even when you deeply disagree. Scripture models it: Jesus asked questions before He answered them, Paul reasoned rather than ridiculed in Athens, and Peter told believers to give reasons with gentleness and respect. It is not compromise - truth still matters - but it refuses contempt, straw men, and the urge to win at the cost of the relationship.

Rest is the God-given rhythm of stopping - weekly Sabbath, nightly sleep, and the deeper rest of a soul that trusts God enough to cease striving. Scripture treats rest as both command and gift: God rested after creation, Jesus invited the weary to come to Him, and Hebrews promises a Sabbath rest still to come. In a culture that measures worth by output, rest is an act of faith: it confesses that the world runs on God's power, not ours.

Restoration is God's work of bringing back what was lost or broken: Israel returned from exile, a ruined life rebuilt, and finally a whole creation made new. The prophets picture it as streams in the desert and dry bones living again, and the New Testament extends it to relationships, bodies, and the cosmos itself. Restoration is larger than repair - it is renewal with interest, the thief repaying sevenfold, the prodigal honored as a son rather than hired as a servant.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall

Summary: Revival is a season when God stirs His people to renewed repentance, prayer, and mission - sometimes sweeping whole regions, as in the Great Awakenings. Scripture's revivals share a pattern: rediscovered truth, conviction of sin, earnest prayer, and fruit that lasts beyond the excitement. Christians pray for revival while remembering it cannot be manufactured: methods can prepare the ground, but only the Spirit gives the increase, and true revival always shows up in changed lives and renewed churches.

Righteousness is right standing before God and right living before people - two sides of one word in Scripture. No one achieves the first by the second: God credits Christ's righteousness to believers by faith, and that gift then produces a life that increasingly does what is right. The prophets and apostles agree: righteousness is both a status received and a calling pursued, and a church that separates them has misunderstood both.
KeyPassages: Genesis 15:6; Psalm 1:1-6; Isaiah 61:10; Romans 3:21-26; Romans 5:17; Philippians 3:7-9

Summary: Sacraments and ordinances are the church's sacred practices: most traditions count baptism and the Lord's Supper, while Catholics and Orthodox add others. Churches differ on what to call them and how they work - means of grace, memorials, or both - but agree they were instituted by Christ and mark belonging to His people. Baptism washes into the new covenant community; the Supper feeds it at the Lord's table; both preach the gospel to the senses.

Satan is the personal, spiritual adversary Scripture calls the accuser, the tempter, and the god of this age - a fallen creature, not God's equal. He appears as the serpent in Eden, the accuser of Job, the tempter of Jesus, and the dragon of Revelation, always working by deception and accusation. Christians take him seriously without fearing him: Christ has disarmed him at the cross, and believers resist him by truth, faith, and the armor of God, knowing his defeat is certain.
KeyPassages: Genesis 3:1-15; Job 1:6-12; Matthew 4:1-11; Ephesians 6:10-18; 1 Peter 5:8-9; Revelation 12:7-12
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Job; Matthew; Ephesians; 1 Peter; Revelation
RelatedEvents: The Fall; Temptation in the Wilderness

Summary: Science and faith meet at the biggest questions: where the universe came from, why it is intelligible, and what humans are for. History shows several models - conflict, independence, dialogue, integration - and Christians hold them with different emphases, from young-earth creation to evolutionary creationism. What unites the conversation is the conviction that truth is one: if God made the world and wrote the Word, careful science and careful exegesis will not finally contradict, even where they currently seem to.
RelatedQuestions: Did God create the world in six literal days?

Summary: Science is the disciplined study of the natural world: observing, testing, and building models that predict how things work. Christians have historically led in science because their worldview expects an orderly creation made by a rational God - and because studying it is a form of worship, not a threat. Science answers how questions with power and precision; it cannot by itself answer why questions about purpose, value, or God, which is why the conflict is often between philosophies, not between science and faith.

Scripture is the written Word of God: sixty-six books that Christians receive as inspired, authoritative, and sufficient for faith and life. It is both human and divine - written by real authors in real cultures, yet breathed out by God - which is why Christians read it historically, literarily, and prayerfully at once. Scripture's center is Christ: the Old Testament anticipates Him, the Gospels present Him, and the Epistles explain what His coming means for the church.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 6:6-9; Psalm 119:97-105; Matthew 4:1-4; Luke 24:27; 2 Timothy 3:14-17; 2 Peter 1:20-21
RelatedDoctrines: Inspiration of Scripture; Inerrancy of Scripture
RelatedBooks: Deuteronomy; Psalms; Matthew; Luke; 2 Timothy; 2 Peter

Summary: Seeking God is the active pursuit of His presence, will, and face - through prayer, Scripture, worship, and obedience. Scripture promises that those who seek Him will find Him, not because seeking earns His favor but because He has already turned toward us. Seeking is both a season and a posture: the desperate search of the lost, the daily discipline of the faithful, and the lifelong journey of people who have tasted and want more.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 4:29; Psalm 27:8; Psalm 63:1; Jeremiah 29:13; Matthew 6:33; Hebrews 11:6

Summary: The soul is the immaterial, enduring part of a human being - the seat of mind, will, and emotion that makes us more than bodies. Scripture speaks of the soul as both the whole person (a living soul) and the part that survives death, held by God until resurrection reunites it with a renewed body. Christians therefore care for souls - their own and others' - as the most valuable thing in the world, worth more than everything else combined.
KeyPassages: Genesis 2:7; Psalm 23:3; Psalm 103:1-5; Matthew 10:28; Mark 8:36; 1 Thessalonians 5:23

Summary: Sovereignty is God's absolute rule over all things: nothing happens outside His knowledge, permission, or purpose. Scripture holds it together with human freedom and moral responsibility without fully resolving the tension, and it anchors comfort: if God is sovereign, suffering is never meaningless and evil never has the last word. The doctrine divides Christians on the details - how God's will relates to human choices - but unites them on the throne: the Lord reigns.
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile

Summary: Spiritual warfare is the Christian's struggle against the world, the flesh, and the devil - a real conflict that is fought with spiritual weapons, not physical ones. Paul's armor of God names the equipment: truth, righteousness, gospel readiness, faith, salvation, and the Word, all wielded in prayer. The battle is already decided at the cross, yet still fiercely contested in daily life, which is why Scripture pairs vigilance with confidence: resist, stand firm, and the enemy will flee.
KeyPassages: Daniel 10:12-14; Matthew 4:1-11; Ephesians 6:10-18; James 4:7; 1 Peter 5:8-9; Revelation 12:7-12
RelatedBooks: Daniel; Matthew; Ephesians; James; 1 Peter; Revelation

Summary: Stereotypes are shortcuts the mind takes about whole groups of people - sometimes with a grain of truth, often with a load of error, always at the cost of seeing individuals. Scripture confronts them directly: Jonah's prejudice against Nineveh, the disciples' contempt for Samaritans, and James's warning against favoritism all show how group labels blind us to neighbors. The gospel answer is particular love: every person bears God's image and deserves to be known before being judged.
RelatedEvents: Jonah and Nineveh; The Good Samaritan; Peter and Cornelius

Summary: Strength in Scripture is rarely self-sufficiency: it is God's power made perfect in human weakness, the quiet endurance of people who keep going because He keeps them. Samson had muscle and failed; Paul had a thorn and triumphed, because strength that depends on God does not run out when our own does. Christians find strength in the same places Israel did - God's promises, His people, and the honest admission that we cannot do this alone.

Superstition is belief in supernatural cause and effect without God's revelation to back it: lucky charms, omens, rituals that manipulate outcomes. It differs from faith because it tries to control the spiritual world rather than trust a personal God, and Scripture groups it with the occult practices Israel was told to leave behind. The cure is not cynicism but confidence: a God who speaks clearly in Scripture and acts wisely in providence leaves no need for secret signs.

Technology is every tool humans make to extend their reach, from plows to smartphones, and Scripture treats tools as morally loaded: useful for good, dangerous when they master us. The Bible's wisdom applies directly - stewardship over addiction, truth over misinformation, presence over distraction, and Sabbath over the endless scroll. Christians neither fear technology nor worship it; they ask of each new tool whether it helps them love God and neighbor better.

Temptation is the pull toward sin, and Scripture is honest about its universality: even Jesus was tempted, though without sin. Temptation itself is not sin - sin enters when we entertain and yield - and God promises both understanding and a way out, since no temptation is unique to us. The practical defenses are ancient: know Scripture, know your weaknesses, avoid the near occasions, confess quickly, and never fight alone.
RelatedEvents: The Fall; Temptation in the Wilderness

Summary: Testimony is telling what God has done, in your life and in history, as evidence for the gospel. The New Testament treats ordinary believers' stories as powerful witness: the healed demoniac sent home to tell his friends, the Samaritan woman bringing her town to Jesus. Good testimony is specific, honest about the before and after, and centered on Christ rather than on the speaker - less look at me and more look at what the Lord has done.
RelatedQuestions: How do I share my faith without being pushy?

Summary: The universe is everything that exists physically: galaxies, stars, planets, and the space and time that contain them. Modern cosmology describes a universe with a beginning, fine-tuned constants, and laws that make science possible - facts Christians read as consistent with a Creator, though not proof of one by themselves. The biblical claim is larger than any theory: the universe is not eternal or self-explaining, but spoken into being by a God who entered it.

Theology is the study of God: what He is like, what He has done, and what He asks of us, drawn from Scripture and organized for understanding. It is not an academic luxury but a practical necessity - everyone is a theologian, because everyone lives by some picture of God, accurate or not. Good theology humbles as much as it informs: it ends, as Paul's does, in worship, because the God it studies is greater than every system built to describe Him.

Tradition is the church's handed-down faith: creeds, liturgies, interpretations, and practices passed from generation to generation. Scripture treats tradition with both respect and suspicion - Paul tells churches to hold to what was delivered, while Jesus rebukes traditions that nullify God's commands. The Reformation's rule remains the test: tradition is a faithful servant when it carries Scripture forward, and a tyrant when it replaces it.

Transformation is the gradual remaking of a person into Christ's likeness, the New Testament's word for what happens after conversion. It is not self-improvement by willpower but renewal by the Spirit: beholding Christ, renewing the mind, and practicing new patterns until they become character. Transformation is slow, uneven, and communal - it happens as we worship, confess, forgive, and serve - and its proof is not perfection but direction: more love, more honesty, more peace than before.

Translation is rendering Scripture from Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek into the languages people actually speak - work the church has done since the Septuagint, three centuries before Christ. Every translation involves interpretation, which is why Christians use several and compare them, and why new translations keep appearing as language changes and manuscripts improve. The doctrine beneath it is confidence: God's Word can be faithfully carried across languages, because its Author intends to be understood.
RelatedDoctrines: Inspiration of Scripture; Inerrancy of Scripture

Summary: True worship is the whole-life response to God's worth: not only songs on Sunday but obedience on Monday, offered in spirit and truth. Jesus told the Samaritan woman that the Father seeks worshipers who worship this way, and the prophets insisted that ritual without justice is noise to God. True worship therefore has two tests: is it directed to the true God, and does it change how we live toward our neighbor?
RelatedQuestions: What is true worship according to the Bible?

Summary: Trust is reliance on God's character when circumstances argue otherwise - the practical shape of faith. Proverbs warns against leaning on our own understanding, the Psalms model trust as refuge-taking, and Jesus sleeps in a storm His disciples fear, showing what trust looks like embodied. Trust grows the way all trust grows: through kept promises remembered, through small obediences, and through suffering that proves God faithful when nothing else holds.
RelatedQuestions: What should I do when my faith feels weak?

Summary: Truth is what corresponds to reality, and in Scripture it is ultimately personal: Jesus calls Himself the truth, and God's Word is described as truth itself. That makes truth-telling a moral duty and truth-seeking a spiritual one - Christians do not get to invent their own facts, and they do not get to hide behind relativism when the truth is costly. The church's witness depends on it: a gospel proclaimed with lies, exaggerations, or half-truths undermines the very message it carries.
KeyPassages: Psalm 119:160; John 1:14; John 8:31-32; John 14:6; John 18:37; Ephesians 4:15

Summary: Victory in Scripture is won, not earned: Israel's battles were God's before they were theirs, and the decisive victory over sin and death belongs to Christ alone. Christians share in it by faith, which is why Paul can call suffering believers more than conquerors in the middle of hardship rather than after it. Victory therefore looks different from triumph: it is endurance, forgiveness, and faithfulness that hold the field because the war's outcome is already settled.
KeyPassages: Exodus 14:13-14; 1 Samuel 17:45-47; John 16:33; Romans 8:35-39; 1 Corinthians 15:54-57; 1 John 5:4-5
RelatedBooks: Exodus; 1 Samuel; John; Romans; 1 Corinthians; 1 John
RelatedEvents: David and Goliath; Fall of Jericho; The Resurrection

Summary: Violence in Scripture is a hard problem Christians must face honestly: the Old Testament contains wars commanded by God, and the New Testament reveals a Savior who absorbs violence rather than inflicting it. Interpreters differ on how to hold these together - some stress progressive revelation, others divine judgment, others the ancient context - but all orthodox readings agree on the trajectory: a world broken by violence, a cross that ends its cycle, and a kingdom where swords become plowshares.
KeyPassages: Genesis 6:11-13; Joshua 6:1-27; Psalm 46:8-10; Matthew 5:38-48; Isaiah 2:2-4; Revelation 21:1-4
RelatedBooks: Genesis; Joshua; Psalms; Matthew; Isaiah; Revelation

Summary: Weakness is the human condition Scripture refuses to romanticize or despise: we are frail, limited, and dependent, and God meets us there rather than waiting for us to get strong. Paul's thorn taught him that grace is sufficient precisely where strength fails, and the church's strength has always come from admitting need rather than hiding it. Weakness is therefore not the opposite of faith but often its clearest evidence: trust is easiest to see when there is nothing else to lean on.

Witness is the church's calling to testify to what God has done, in words and in life. The legal metaphor is deliberate: witnesses do not invent the case, they report what they have seen and heard, and the Spirit makes the testimony effective. Witness takes many forms - a shared story, a defended hope, a life that makes the gospel plausible - but its center is always Jesus: His death, resurrection, and the new life He gives.
RelatedQuestions: How do I share my faith without being pushy?

Summary: The Word of God is God's self-revelation: Christ Himself, the living Word, and Scripture, the written Word that testifies to Him. Christians distinguish the two without separating them - the written Word's authority flows from the living Word it proclaims. To call the Bible God's Word is to claim it speaks with His voice: it creates, convicts, comforts, and commands, and it stands as the church's final court of appeal.
RelatedDoctrines: Inspiration of Scripture; Inerrancy of Scripture

Summary: Word studies are the careful examination of biblical words in their original languages, tracing how Hebrew and Greek terms are used across Scripture. Done well, they unlock precision - the difference between kinds of love, or what covenant meant to its first hearers - and done badly, they mislead, as when a word's root is mistaken for its meaning. Word studies serve the church best when they stay humble: words get their meaning from sentences, sentences from books, and books from the whole canon.

World religions are the great faith traditions alongside Christianity - Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, and others - each with its own scriptures, practices, and picture of ultimate reality. Christians approach them with both respect and conviction: respect for the people who hold them and the truths they contain, and conviction that Jesus Christ is the unique Son of God and the only Savior. Understanding other faiths fairly matters for honest witness, good neighboring, and answering the question of why Christians believe what they do.

A worldview is the set of assumptions through which a person interprets everything: what is real, what is true, what is right, and what humans are for. Everyone has one, whether examined or not, and the Christian worldview - creation, fall, redemption, restoration - offers a coherent alternative to naturalism, pantheism, and relativism. Christians study worldviews to understand their neighbors, to test their own thinking, and to show how the gospel answers the deepest questions every worldview must face.
